title: Compete in good
hookLine: to each We gave a law and a way; had Allah willed He'd have made one community, so race in good (5:48)
last: ONE LIFE — ONE LIFE, ALL LIFE.

cards: A friendly race can look like this. Two coworkers trying to be first to cover a shift for someone sick. Two sisters each sneaking off to pay the restaurant bill before the other can.

Nobody loses, exactly; the point is the thing being raced toward. Surah five has spent several verses on earlier scriptures: the Torah, which it calls guidance and light, then the Gospel given to Isa, then the Qur'an.
Then it reaches a verse that asks why there are different communities at all, and gives an answer shaped like a race.

teach.h: SHIR'AH — THE PATH DOWN TO WATER.
teach.b: Verse forty-eight, in Pickthall's words: “For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way.” Two Arabic words there.
Shir'ah, from the same root as shari'ah, which Arabic lexicons say first named the path down to a watering place, the trail people and animals walk to reach water. And minhaj, a clear, open road.
Then: had Allah willed, He could have made you one community. But He didn't, so that He may test you in what He has given you. And then the turn: “So vie one with another in good works.”
The Arabic is fastabiqu al-khayrat: race each other toward the good things. The same command appears in surah two.

teach.h: HE WILL TELL YOU WHERE YOU DIFFERED.
teach.b: The verse ends by saying everyone returns to Allah, and He will tell them about the things they differed over. Muslim scholars read this in more than one way.

teach.h: VIE ONE WITH ANOTHER IN GOOD WORKS.
teach.b: Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir understood it as each prophet's community receiving its law in its own time, with the Qur'an now the law for Muslims and a guardian over the earlier books.
Some Muslim writers today stress the second half: the differences are real, and their settling belongs to God, on the Day, not to us now. Both readings share the practical point.
While people differ, the verse doesn't say argue until someone wins. It says race toward the good. Your neighbor's kindness is not a threat to yours.
It's the pace you're trying to match.

how: Muslims often quote fastabiqu al-khayrat (2:148; 5:48) to encourage charity drives and good works, and 5:48 is often cited when speaking about living alongside people of other faiths.

games.why: vie one with another in good works. the verse leaves the settling of differences to Allah, when everyone returns to Him.

practice: Somewhere near you is a person who is better at one kind of good: they remember birthdays, or visit the sick, or never gossip.
Without guilt, let them be a runner just ahead of you, and picture the one call, one gift, or one silence where gossip would have gone that would help you catch up.
